author: Goethe
title: The changing measures of Faust
where: *Faust*, Part I: the Prologue in Heaven, the first Study scene and Gretchen’s room
about: In Heaven three archangels end their hymn to the Lord’s creation, and Mephistopheles, the devil of the play, speaks next. In the second passage he has come into the study of the scholar Faust, first as a poodle and then as a traveling scholar, and Faust asks who he is. In the third, Gretchen, the girl Faust has courted with the devil’s help, sits alone at her spinning wheel. Faust has kissed her and has since gone off into the forest. The English printed here calls her Margaret.

view.says: Auden thought *Faust* rich in poetry and in wise sayings but not exciting as drama. He likened it to a variety show: the scenes are of interest one by one and have no real continuity. No translation, he wrote, can show how many styles of poetry Goethe commanded. Auden’s own age, he held, worships possibility, and the Devil of such an age comes as Mephisto, that is, as an actor, to whom no name belongs.
view.quote: Goethe’s amazing command of every style of poetry, from the coarse to the witty to the lyrical to the sublime
view.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 115 and 118; “Italian Journey,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 131

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: four beats to the line for the archangels; five beats, then six, for Mephistopheles; the line beginning off the beat throughout

points.say: The three archangels end their hymn. Each of its lines has four beats, in nine syllables and eight by turns.
From here Mephistopheles is speaking, four lines into his speech, in five beats. *Hohe Worte*: high words.
The voice starts on a stress and passes over the first beat. The line can also be said with the stress on *du*, you.
Six beats, with a pause after the third.

lenses.why: The measure changes where the speaker changes: the archangels keep the four-beat stanza of their hymn, and Mephistopheles, who says he cannot make high words, speaks the mixed rhymed lines in which the Lord then answers him.
lenses.caption: The first four lines end the archangels’ hymn: four beats a line, as in the twenty-four before. With Mephistopheles the measure changes. Here he has six lines of five beats, then two of six that break in the middle; the rest of his speech mixes four, five and six. The Lord answers him in the same mixed lines, which are the verse of most of the play. In his first line here Mephistopheles says he cannot make hohe Worte, high words: fine phrases like the archangels’, as an edition of 1892 explains them.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. A count of the beats in the hymn, in Mephistopheles’ speech and in the Lord’s reply, lines 243 to 295 of the German: [the Prologue in Heaven](#/read/faust/prologue:13). That most of the play is in this mixed verse: Bayard Taylor’s preface, and German Wikipedia under *Madrigalvers*. High words: Calvin Thomas’s edition of 1892, note on line 275.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.why: Rhyme by turns runs through the hymn and the devil’s excuse; at his subject he turns to pairs, and the pair that judges man, one closed sentence, lands on the hymn’s own rhyme and its last word, day.
lenses.caption: The letters at the line ends mark the rhymes. The hymn rhymes by turns: Stärke with Werke, mag with Tag. Mephistopheles keeps that order while he excuses himself. When he comes to his subject, how men torment themselves, he changes to pairs and stays in pairs to the end of his speech. A rhyme that returns at once makes its two lines one unit, able to hold one complete idea. His second pair is one sentence, and it says what he thinks of man. Its rhyme, Schlag, stamp or kind, with Tag, is the rhyme the hymn ended on, and Tag, day, is the hymn’s last word.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. The rest of Mephistopheles’ speech, which keeps to pairs: [the Prologue in Heaven](#/read/faust/prologue:11). That a rhyme returning at once makes its two lines one unit: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on the short couplet. *Schlag*: the *Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache*.

lenses.label: Parody
lenses.name: parody
lenses.plain: the form and wording of a dignified piece closely imitated and made ridiculous by an unfitting subject
lenses.why: Mephistopheles keeps the hymn’s closing words, as on the first day, and its word high, and changes what they are said of: glorious works become odd man, and the Lord hears an accusation.
lenses.caption: The hymn ends on wie am ersten Tag, as on the first day. The Lord’s hohen Werke, high works, are herrlich, glorious, as on that day. The archangel Raphael’s stanza, the hymn’s first, ended on the same line, so the hymn says it twice. Mephistopheles takes the words up. He says he cannot make hohe Worte, high words, and that man is wunderlich, odd, as on the first day. He keeps the line’s end and changes the adjective. That is parody. An edition of 1892 notes that his line parodies the hymn’s. When he ends, the Lord asks whether he always comes only to accuse.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. The line that ends Raphael’s stanza and [the Lord’s question](#/read/faust/prologue:13) are in the Prologue as printed here; where Goethe has a word for accusing, Taylor’s English has *ill intention*. *Herrlich* and *wunderlich*: the *Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache*. Parody as the Online Etymology Dictionary defines it. Calvin Thomas’s edition of 1892, notes on lines 275 and 282.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: As on the first day: Taylor has *Creation’s hour*.
The same four German words as at the hymn’s close; in English *hour* becomes *day*.
High works: Taylor has *sublime and splendid*.
Taylor’s first two lines stand in the opposite order to Goethe’s.

lenses.why: Taylor keeps the beats and the order of the rhymes, and the exact returns on which the parody turns come out loosened; Auden held that no translation shows how many styles Goethe commanded.
lenses.caption: Auden wrote that no translation can show how many styles of poetry Goethe commanded. Under each German line stands Bayard Taylor’s English of 1870. His title page says in the original metres, and he keeps Goethe’s beats line for line, four, then five, then six, and the order of the rhymes. The words Goethe repeats come out looser. Goethe ends two lines on the same four words; Taylor has Creation’s hour, then Creation’s day, and his last pair no longer rhymes with the hymn’s close. Hohen Werke and hohe Worte become works, sublime and splendid and lofty speech.
lenses.stands: The two versions as they stand, line under line. Taylor’s title page and preface, on keeping the original meters. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 131.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: rhymed lines of six, five and four beats, the line beginning off the beat

points.say: Faust speaks. Six beats, and the line breaks after the first of the three names.
Faust’s question is half a line. Mephistopheles’ first words, just below, are the other half: six beats between the two speakers.
The riddle: six beats, breaking after *will*, wills.
Faust again, in five beats. *Gemeint*, meant, waits for its rhyme in the answer: *verneint*.

lenses.why: The riddle comes in the six-beat line that divides into two equal halves, which Schiller told Goethe puts French plays under the rule of opposition; asked what it means, Mephistopheles begins his answer in four beats.
lenses.caption: Faust’s line of three names has six beats and breaks in the middle. His question and Mephistopheles’ first words make a second such line, and the next line, the riddle, is a third. This is the alexandrine, the long line of French verse. Schiller wrote to Goethe in 1799 that it divides into two equal halves and rhymes in pairs, and that this puts everything in the French plays under the rule of opposition. Faust asks what the riddle means, and the answer begins in four beats: der Geist, der stets verneint, the spirit who always says no. Six of the answer’s seven lines have four beats.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The alexandrine: *Meyers Großes Konversations-Lexikon* under *Alexandriner*, and Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4. Schiller’s letter to Goethe of 15 October 1799, which is about French plays in translation. The lines themselves.

lenses.label: Antithesis
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.why: The line’s matching halves set what this power wills against what it brings about, and Faust calls it a riddle; Auden, quoting it, could hardly see any good or evil that Mephisto does to Faust.
lenses.caption: The riddle’s line has two halves built alike: stets, always, then a noun, then a verb. Das Böse, evil, stands against das Gute, good, and will, wills, against schafft, works. Contraries set close in matching words are an antithesis. It sets what the power wants against what it brings about; Faust calls it a riddle. In the Prologue the Lord used this verb of the companion he gives man, who must, as devil, schaffen. Auden quoted those lines in 1941 and wrote that the Devil brings about the loss of his own wager. Later, quoting the riddle, he could hardly see any good or evil that Mephisto does to Faust.
lenses.stands: The marks on the line, and Faust’s question after it. Antithesis as the Online Etymology Dictionary and *Silva Rhetoricae* define it; the German words from the *Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache*. The Lord’s lines are in [the Prologue in Heaven](#/read/faust/prologue:37), where Taylor’s English has *create* for *schaffen*. Auden: “The Wandering Jew,” *The New Republic*, 10 February 1941, and *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 117.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: Goethe’s German for *Beelzebub*, lord of the fly: a Philistine god’s name, which the New Testament gives to the prince of devils.
The Destroyer of Revelation 9:11: *Abaddon* in Hebrew, *Apollyon* in Greek.
In John 8:44 the devil is a liar and the father of lying.
German *Rätsel* and English *riddle* are one old Germanic word.
Made from *nein*, no. Grimm’s dictionary sets this line beside the Lord’s line in the Prologue about the spirits who deny.
Word for word: goes to the ground.
*Eigentlich* is made from *eigen*, own. A person’s *Element* is the surroundings that suit him.

lenses.why: Asked his name, the devil gives a description, the spirit who always says no; Auden named the Devil by this line in 1941, and later wrote that a spirit rejecting everything actual must hate creation.
lenses.caption: Faust has asked Mephistopheles his name and got no answer. He cites three names for devils. Two put Bible names into German: Fliegengott, god of flies, is Beelzebub, and Verderber, destroyer, is Apollyon. Lügner, liar, is what John’s Gospel calls the devil. The answer takes none of them. It gives ein Teil, a part, then a description: der Geist, der stets verneint, the spirit who always says no. In New Year Letter (1941) Auden names the Devil by this line in English, and his note gives the German. He later wrote that a spirit which rejects everything actual must hate creation; here Mephistopheles says that all that comes to be, entsteht, deserves to perish.
lenses.stands: The lines themselves, with Faust’s question and the first reply just before them in [the first Study scene](#/read/faust/s03:29). The three names: Calvin Thomas’s edition of 1892, note on line 1334, with Revelation 9:11 and John 8:44. The glosses: the *Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache* and Grimm’s *Deutsches Wörterbuch*. Auden: *New Year Letter* (1941), line 384 and its note, and *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 117.

lenses.label: Names
lenses.what: what Mephistopheles is called in Part I, and what he comes as

facts.in English: the poodle’s core: the scholar inside the poodle
god of flies, destroyer, liar: what devils are called
the spirit who always says no
Squire Satan; he forbids the name
Baron, as he asks to be called
Squire Voland, an old name of the devil
a noble squire: red coat trimmed with gold, cloak of stiff silk, cock’s feather, long sword
the mask, his costume: Faust’s gown and cap
to play the devil, said aside

lenses.why: Auden says the Devil of an age that worships possibility is an actor, to whom no name belongs; in Part I nobody speaks the name Mephistopheles, he refuses the name Satan, and he calls Faust’s gown his costume.
lenses.caption: Auden wrote that in Mephisto the Devil comes as an actor, and that no name belongs to an actor: his name is Legion, the name of the many devils in the Gospel. In Part I the name Mephistopheles stands over more than 250 speeches and nobody speaks it. Faust says the short form, Mephisto, once. The Lord calls him der Schalk, the rogue. A witch greets him as Junker Satan, Squire Satan; he forbids the name and asks to be called Baron. He comes as a poodle, a traveling scholar and a squire in red. In Faust’s gown, which he calls die Maske, his costume, he says aside that he must play the devil again.
lenses.stands: A count of the name in the German text and in the English printed here: speech headings, stage directions and spoken lines. The places: [the Lord’s word for him](#/read/faust/prologue:37), [the traveling scholar](#/read/faust/s03:22), [the squire’s dress](#/read/faust/s04:12), [Faust’s gown and cap](#/read/faust/s04:95), [Squire Satan](#/read/faust/s06:109) and [Mephisto](#/read/faust/s21:173). *Maske*: the *Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache*. Legion is the many devils’ name in Mark 5:9. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 118.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: two beats to the line, in lines of three to six syllables

points.say: Gretchen speaks, alone. Two beats, one thing to a line.
One word fills the line: *Zauberfluß*, magic flow. The item began in the line above.
*Kuß*, the kiss. The list ends here, with no verb.
The first stanza of the scene comes back, for the second time.

lenses.why: Two beats give each thing of his a line to itself; at the kiss the list stops without a verb and the opening stanza of the scene returns word for word.
lenses.caption: Every line here can be said with two beats, and so can every line of the scene, forty in all. Goethe’s direction does not say that she sings; Schubert made a song of the scene in 1814. A line holds one thing of Faust’s: his walk, his figure, his smile, his eyes. One item runs over: seiner Rede Zauberfluß, the magic flow of his talk, is cut in two, and its second line is a single word. After sein Kuß, his kiss, the sentence stops without a verb, and the scene’s first stanza comes back word for word, as it did once before.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. A count of beats and syllables in the forty lines of the scene in the German, and a comparison of its first, fourth and eighth stanzas. The stage direction at the head of [Gretchen’s room](#/read/faust/s15:1). Schubert’s song: German Wikipedia, under *Gretchen am Spinnrade*.

lenses.label: Anaphora
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same word at the head of line after line
lenses.why: The possessive at the head of the items makes the seven things that are his one list without a verb, running to the kiss and stopping there; the stanza that returns begins with my and I.
lenses.caption: Seven things of Faust’s are named in eight lines. Five begin with sein, his, at the head of the line; two have it after und, and. A word repeated at the head of line after line is anaphora; it makes the items a list, here without a verb. The list goes from his walk, figure, smile and eyes to his talk and then to touch: Händedruck, the pressure of his hand, and Kuß, the kiss. There it stops, and the returning stanza begins Meine, Mein, Ich: my, my, I.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Anaphora as *Silva Rhetoricae* and the Online Etymology Dictionary define it. The German words: the *Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache* and Grimm’s *Deutsches Wörterbuch*, which cites this line under *Händedruck*.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Taylor keeps *His* at the head of the first two lines.
From the third line on, *his* moves inside the line, and *The*, *And*, *Of* or *In* stands first.
*Gestalt* is a person’s figure or build. Taylor has *size*, which rhymes with *eyes*.
*Zauberfluß*: magic flow. Taylor turns the two lines round, the flow first and the talk after.
*Händedruck*: the pressure of a hand. Before it Taylor has *the bliss*, which is not in the German and gives him the rhyme for *kiss*.
The kiss ends the list in both.

lenses.why: Taylor keeps the beats and the rhymes and gives up the repeated possessive at the head of the lines; Auden wrote that in translation Goethe is likely to seem too intellectual and short of passion.
lenses.caption: Taylor keeps the two beats in every line and the rhyme of each stanza’s second and fourth lines. What he gives up is the repeated word. Goethe’s sein heads five of the eight lines; Taylor’s His heads two, and then The, And, Of and In take its place. Size stands for Gestalt, a person’s figure, and the bliss is not in the German; both appear to be there for the rhymes with eyes and kiss. A reader who knows Faust only in translation, Auden wrote, will probably think Goethe too intellectual and short of passion.
lenses.stands: The two versions as they stand, line under line. *Gestalt*: the *Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache*. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 131.

lenses.label: Measures
lenses.what: nine of the measures of Part I, each with a place to read it

facts.in plain words: stanzas of eight five-beat lines, rhymed a b a b a b c c
four beats to a line, nine and eight syllables by turns, rhymed by turns
rhymed lines of changing length, here of four, five and six beats in no fixed order: the verse of the greater part of the play
four beats in eight to eleven syllables, rhymed mostly in pairs: the verse of Hans Sachs and the sixteenth century
six beats with a break in the middle, mixed into the dialogue
five beats to a line, without rhyme
ten stanzas of four lines, the first returning twice
the one scene of Part I not in verse

lenses.why: The verse of Part I changes measure with scene and speaker, from the eight-line stanza to prose; Auden compared the play to a variety show and wrote that Goethe commanded every style of poetry.
lenses.caption: Auden likened Faust to a variety show: one scene after another, each of interest in itself. The verse keeps changing too. Part I opens in ottava rima, the eight-line stanza of the Italian epics. The archangels’ hymn has four beats. Faust’s first speech opens in Knittelvers, the four-beat rhymed line that ruled German verse in the sixteenth century, when the first book about Faust was printed. Most of the play is in rhymed lines of changing length. Gretchen sings a song in three beats; Faust, alone in the forest, speaks unrhymed lines of five; Gretchen at her wheel has two beats; and one scene is prose.
lenses.stands: A count of beats, syllables and rhymes in the German text at each place named. The measures and their histories: *Meyers Großes Konversations-Lexikon* under *Stanze* and *Knüttelverse*, Calvin Thomas’s edition of 1892, German Wikipedia under *Madrigalvers*. Places to read: [the Dedication](#/read/faust/dedication:0), [Faust’s first speech](#/read/faust/s01:2), [“The King of Thule”](#/read/faust/s08:43), [Forest and Cavern](#/read/faust/s14:2), [Dreary Day](#/read/faust/s23:3). Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 115.

auden.says: In February 1941 Auden reviewed three books of Kafka and turned the review into a history of the hero who goes on a quest. With *Faust*, he wrote, something new comes into the story that *Pilgrim’s Progress* did not have: irony. He quoted the Lord’s lines about the companion who must work as a devil, and concluded that the Devil himself brings about the loss of his wager. Faust and Peer Gynt, he added, are exceptional for being morally worse than ordinary people; God and men favor them because they take what is arbitrary in themselves for what is necessary.
auden.quote: Faust is saved because he is never content, and he is never content because Mephistopheles will never let him rest
auden.source: “The Wandering Jew,” *The New Republic*, 10 February 1941; reprinted in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 110–13

auden.says: Auden could well imagine every actor wanting the part of Mephisto, who never fails to entertain, while whoever plays Faust goes unnoticed as long as Mephisto is on stage. He blamed the play’s faults as drama on the myth itself and held that Goethe did not lack talent as a dramatist. Faust’s story, as he read it, is about a man who will not be anyone and wants only to turn into someone else, and Mephisto makes visible what is possible and not actual. In an ideal production, he said, identical twins would play the two.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 115–16

auden.says: Mephisto calls himself a part of the part that was once everything. Auden read this as a refusal of everything finite: a spirit that turns down whatever is actual can only hate creation. Of the riddle shown here he said he could hardly tell what good or what evil Mephisto does to Faust. With his help Faust may do others a great deal of harm, but nothing Faust does alters Faust. He lets Mephisto entertain him, and these shows change his character as little as watching the play changes its audience.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 117

auden.says: Auden held that Faust escapes damnation and yet cannot sensibly be called saved: the angels who carry him to Heaven speak of him as still a pupa, and a creature in that state cannot be judged. In 1946 he found the ending of the play unsatisfying as art: the reader does not believe that Faust is saved, and neither, he thought, does Goethe. In 1948 he wrote that Marlowe, though less clever than Goethe, had the sounder sense, since his Faustus ends in hell.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 117; “K.’s Quest,” in *The Kafka Problem*, edited by Angel Flores (1946), p. 49; “Squares and Oblongs,” in *Poets at Work* (1948), reprinted in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 349–50

auden.says: In class in December 1941, lecturing on *The Tempest*, Auden said that Prospero’s giving up of his magic for ordinary life belongs to a very old theme, and that Faust gives up something like it. Faust lets go of wide learning and power so that he can be of direct use to other people, in his case by joining in the building of dikes. The reference is to the end of Part II. This comes from notes a student made after the lecture.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 150

auden.says: In *New Year Letter*, the long poem he published in 1941, Auden names the Devil by Mephistopheles’ line, put into English, and a note gives the German and cites *Faust*, Part I, Scene 3. A little later the poem addresses Mephistopheles as one who has been cheated and only thinks he is having his own way. Another note quotes, in German, the Lord’s lines about the companion who must work as a devil.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (London: Faber, 1941), lines 384 and 400, with the notes to lines 384 and 395

auden.says: Writing of the Romantic hero and his lack of any lasting interest in other people, Auden set Faust beside Ibsen’s Peer Gynt. Each comes across a great many people, and what matters about both, he said, is that they go on and the others stay where they were.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), p. 107

sources: The German: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, *Faust. Der Tragödie erster Teil* (first printed 1808), in the modern-spelling text of Project Gutenberg (no. 2229), with the line numbers of the standard editions.
The English under it, and the copy to read here: *Faust*, Part I, translated in the original metres by Bayard Taylor (1870), as Project Gutenberg prints it (no. 14591), with Taylor’s preface.
The first edition, used for the numbering of the lines: *Faust. Eine Tragödie* (Tübingen: Cotta, 1808), as transcribed at German Wikisource.

*Goethes Faust*, edited by Calvin Thomas, vol. I: The First Part (Boston: D. C. Heath, 1892): introduction, p. xxxviii; the notes on the Dedication, the Prelude and the name Mephistopheles; on lines 275, 282, 339, 1334, 1336 and 4023; and on Gretchen’s room.

W. H. Auden, “K.’s Quest,” in *The Kafka Problem*, edited by Angel Flores (1946), p. 49, and “Squares and Oblongs,” in *Poets at Work* (1948), reprinted in *Prose*, vol. II, pp. 349–50. Not seen in full.

caveats: Auden names no passages for the styles he lists, and does not point to the names and costumes of Mephistopheles; his variety show is a remark about the scenes. The passages and these matchings are this page’s choice, as is setting Schiller’s remark on French plays beside the riddle.

The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing of the German. Another reader could fairly mark some syllables otherwise, above all the first words of lines, and some of Gretchen’s lines can be heard with three beats.

An editor of 1892 reads the riddle as the devil’s own opinion: in doing what men call bad he does what he thinks good, and admits no higher power that turns it to good. He finds no special effect meant in the six-beat lines of the Prelude at the Theatre.

Auden’s article of 1941, his notes to *New Year Letter* and his essays of 1946 and 1948 were read here only in snippets of scanned copies. What he said in class comes from notes a student, Donald Pearce, made after the lectures.

The course’s reading list names the Everyman edition, which is Albert Latham’s translation, and “Omit” is written by hand against the title. The English here is Bayard Taylor’s. The German is a modern-spelling text and not the spelling of 1808.
